natural-selection-intro-s1.title: Coat color and survival in outdoor enclosures
natural-selection-intro-s1.html:
In a species of mouse, coat color is either light or dark. Researchers built eight identical outdoor enclosures, four with light sandy soil and four with dark soil. Into each enclosure they released 10 light-coated and 10 dark-coated adult mice of the same age and size. In six enclosures, owls that hunt at night could fly in; two enclosures (one of each soil) were covered with netting that kept owls out. After four weeks the researchers trapped every surviving mouse. Results for the enclosures of each kind were combined.

natural-selection-intro-s2.title: Lifetime reproduction of a meadow plant with three flower colors
natural-selection-intro-s2.html:
A meadow plant has white, pink or purple flowers, and flower color is inherited. Researchers marked 50 plants of each color in one meadow and counted the seeds each plant made. They then followed every seed to see whether it grew into a plant that flowered the next year. Purple plants made the largest seeds and pink plants the smallest.

natural-selection-s1.title: Beak depth of island finches across a drought and a wet year
natural-selection-s1.html:
On a small island, researchers banded and measured nearly every member of a population of seed-eating finches each year. Earlier work there had shown that beak depth is heritable: chicks resemble their parents in beak depth whatever they are fed. In 1977 almost no rain fell. The small, soft seeds were eaten first, the remaining seeds were mostly large and hard, and about 85% of the finches died; no chicks were raised that year. In 1983 heavy rain produced a flood of small, soft seeds that lasted two years. Each point is the mean beak depth of the birds hatched in that year, measured once they were adults, with error bars of ± 2 SE. (Values are simplified for teaching.)

natural-selection-s2.title: Tail length and mating success in a grassland bird
natural-selection-s2.html:
In a grassland bird, males have tails about half a meter long, several times longer than the females' tails. Researchers caught 36 males that each held a territory, and assigned 9 at random to each of four groups. Shortened: tail cut to about 15 cm. Cut and reglued: tail cut and the same feathers glued back, so length was unchanged. Unaltered: caught, measured and released. Lengthened: feathers taken from the shortened birds glued on, adding about 25 cm. The researchers then counted the new nests that females built in each male's territory over the next four weeks.

artificial-selection-s1.title: Selecting corn for high and low oil content
artificial-selection-s1.html:
In a long-running breeding experiment, researchers started two lines from the same variety of corn, whose kernels averaged 4.7% oil. Every generation they measured the oil content of the kernels on many ears. In the high line they planted only kernels from the 12 ears with the most oil; in the low line, only kernels from the 12 ears with the least. All plants were grown in the same fields. The graph shows the mean oil content of each line every 10 generations (values rounded).

artificial-selection-s2.html:

Three flasks (untreated) received none. Every day, 1% of each culture was moved into a fresh flask of the same medium. Every six days the researchers measured the MIC, the lowest antibiotic concentration that stops a sample of the culture from growing.

population-genetics-s1.title: Allele frequency over generations in small and large populations
population-genetics-s1.html:
Researchers set up five laboratory populations of fruit flies from one stock in which the frequency of an eye-color allele, e, was 0.50. The allele has no known effect on survival or reproduction in the lab. Each generation, a set number of adults was taken at random to be the parents of the next generation: 10 adults in each of the small populations S1, S2 and S3, and 500 adults in each of the large populations L1 and L2. All populations were kept on the same food at the same temperature. The graph shows the frequency of e among the parents of each generation.

population-genetics-s2.title: A shrinking population of grassland birds
population-genetics-s2.html:
A grassland bird once lived across a whole state. As its prairie was plowed, one remaining population became cut off from all others by many kilometers of farmland. Researchers counted displaying males each spring, recorded the percentage of eggs that hatched in nests they monitored, and estimated genetic variation from the average number of alleles per gene at six genes, using DNA from feathers. Between 1992 and 1996 they released 270 birds caught in three large populations in other states. (Values are simplified for teaching.)

hardy-weinberg-s1.title: Genotype counts in three plant populations
hardy-weinberg-s1.html:
A wildflower species has a gene with two codominant alleles, A and a, so every genotype can be identified from the plants' flower-pigment pattern. Researchers counted 500 flowering adults in each of three populations. Population X grows in a large meadow and is pollinated by bees. Population Y grows on a cliff where bees are rare, and most of its seeds come from flowers that pollinated themselves. Population Z grows on soil where, in seedling surveys, AA and aa seedlings were seen to die more often than Aa seedlings.

hardy-weinberg-s2.title: Frequency of a recessive allele in four laboratory populations
hardy-weinberg-s2.html:
Researchers founded four populations of flour beetles from one stock in which the frequency (q) of a recessive allele, a, was 0.50. Beetles with genotype aa have a reddish body; AA and Aa beetles look the same. Each population was treated differently for 20 generations. Population 1: 2,000 breeding adults, nothing else done. Population 2: 2,000 breeding adults, but every reddish (aa) beetle was removed before it could breed. Population 3: 2,000 breeding adults, but each generation 10% of the breeders were replaced by beetles from a stock in which q = 0.10. Population 4: 10 breeding adults chosen at random each generation.

evolution-evidence-s2.title: Rock layers in a canyon wall
evolution-evidence-s2.html:
Geologists described six undisturbed layers exposed in a canyon wall, numbered from the top. Three layers are volcanic ash, whose crystals were dated by the decay of a radioactive isotope. The other layers are sedimentary rock containing fossils of horse-like mammals.

items.q: Which statement best describes the results?
options: With owls, mice matching the soil survived at about twice the rate of mismatched mice; without owls, both coats survived well.
Light-coated mice survived better than dark-coated mice on both soils, whether or not the owls could reach them to hunt.
With owls present, survival was similar for both coats, but it differed between coats once the owls were kept out.
Dark soil lowered the survival of both coat colors compared with light sand, with or without owls.

items.q: For the light-sand enclosures with owls, calculate the survival of dark-coated mice relative to light-coated mice (proportion of dark mice surviving ÷ proportion of light mice surviving). Give your answer to two decimal places.
Why did the researchers include enclosures covered with netting?
options: To test whether owls cause the survival differences, with everything else kept the same
To find out which coat color owls prefer to eat when they are offered both colors at once
To let the mice breed undisturbed so that the coat colors of their offspring could be counted
To measure how much the coats of the protected mice changed color during the four weeks

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for why survival depended on the match between coat and soil?
options: Owls hunt by sight, so they find mice that contrast with the ground more often and catch more of them.
Mice on soil that matched their coat found more food, so they were stronger and escaped owls more often.
Mice that sensed they did not match the soil stayed hidden, so the owls caught the matching mice instead.
The soil color changed how fast each mouse's coat grew, and slow coat growth made mice easier to catch.

items.q: Coat color in this species is inherited. A wild population of these mice on light sand starts with 50% dark-coated mice, and owls keep killing mice at the rates in the table. Which prediction is best supported?
options: Over generations the percentage of dark mice falls, because dark mice leave fewer surviving offspring.
Dark mice gradually grow lighter coats as they spend more of their lives on light sand.
The percentage of dark mice stays at 50%, because coat color is set by alleles, not by owls.
Dark mice vanish from the population in a single generation, because 67% of them die.

items.q: Using flowering offspring per plant as the measure of fitness, calculate the relative fitness of white-flowered plants. Give your answer to two decimal places.
A student claims that pink-flowered plants have the highest fitness because they make the most seeds. Which response is best supported by the data?
options: Fitness counts offspring that survive to reproduce, and pink plants leave the fewest: 5.0 each.
The claim is right, because seed number is the standard way biologists measure the fitness of a plant.
The claim is right for this year, because the seeds of pink plants will have more chances to grow next year.
Pink plants have the lowest fitness because their seeds are small, and small seeds rarely sprout.

items.q: If conditions in the meadow stay the same for many generations, which change in the population is most likely?
options: Purple-flowered plants become a larger share of the population.
Pink-flowered plants become a larger share, because they make the most seeds.
The shares of the three colors stay the same, because the plants grow side by side in one meadow.
White-flowered plants become the largest share, because they are intermediate in both seed number and survival.

items.q: In a dry year, the percentage of seeds that grow into flowering plants is cut in half for all three colors equally. How does this affect the relative fitness of white-flowered plants?
options: It stays at 0.75, because every color's offspring number falls by the same factor.
It falls to about 0.38, because white plants leave half as many offspring.
It rises toward 1, because a harsh year makes the colors more alike.
It can no longer be calculated, because no color reaches its usual number of offspring.

items.q: Which conditions are needed for natural selection to change a trait in a population? Select ALL that apply.
options: Individuals differ in the trait.
The differences are at least partly inherited.
The differences affect survival or reproduction.
Individuals sense which version of the trait would help them.
The environment directs mutations toward the helpful trait.
Each offspring born survives to reproduce.

items.q: Put the steps of natural selection in a population of beetles on dark soil in order.
options: Beetles differ in color, and color is inherited.
More beetles hatch than the soil can feed, and birds hunt them.
Birds catch more light beetles, which stand out on dark soil.
Dark survivors leave more offspring than light survivors.
The next generation has a higher proportion of dark beetles.

items.q: An old explanation for giraffes' long necks says that each giraffe stretched its neck to reach high leaves, its neck grew a little longer, and its offspring inherited the longer neck. What is the main flaw in this explanation?
options: Changes made to the body during life do not alter the DNA in gametes, so they are not inherited.
Giraffes could not have stretched their necks, because the length of a neck is fixed at birth.
It leaves out mutation, which on its own would lengthen the necks of a whole herd within one generation.
Acquired traits can be inherited, but neck length is too complex a trait to be passed to offspring.

items.q: Which deer has the highest fitness?
options: A small male that lives 4 years and fathers 7 fawns that survive to breed
A large male that lives 15 years and fathers 3 fawns that survive to breed
A female that lives 12 years and gives birth to 10 fawns, 2 of which survive to breed
A male that wins the most fights in the herd and fathers 1 fawn that survives to breed

items.q: In a mountain hare population, fur thickness is heritable. Thick fur helped hares survive cold winters, but a long run of warm winters begins, and thick-furred hares now overheat and leave fewer young. Predict the effect of many warm winters on each of these.

variables.name: Proportion of newborn hares with thick fur, many generations later
Number of surviving young left by a thick-furred hare compared with a thin-furred hare
Number of copies of the thick-fur allele in each cell of a thick-furred adult that survives
Average fur thickness of the population, many generations later

items.q: After a hurricane swept over a small island, the lizards that survived had larger toe pads, on average, than lizards measured on the island just before the storm. Which additional finding would best support the claim that the population evolved?
options: The survivors' offspring, raised in the same conditions as earlier lizards' offspring, also have larger toe pads.
The survivors' toe pads grew larger in the months after the storm, as they climbed in damaged trees.
Lizards with large toe pads were seen clinging to branches during the storm while others were blown away.
The survivors were older, and so had larger bodies and feet, on average, than the lizards measured before the storm.

items.q: What did Charles Darwin mean by "descent with modification"?
options: Species living today descend from earlier species and have changed over many generations.
Each individual modifies its traits during life and passes the changes to its offspring.
Species were formed separately and have stayed the same since they first appeared.
Individuals change over their lifetimes, while species themselves stay unchanged.

items.q: A female cod can release millions of eggs a year, yet a cod population can stay roughly the same size for decades. Which conclusion follows?
options: Almost all offspring die before reproducing, as young fish compete for limited resources or are eaten.
Cod release more eggs in years when the population is small and fewer when it is large.
Most eggs go unfertilized, so the number of young that hatch matches the number of adults that die each year.
The high egg number shows that cod have higher fitness than fish that release fewer eggs.

items.q: No beetle in a population can digest a plant that contains a certain toxin. A fire destroys the beetles' other food plants, leaving the toxic plant. What is the most likely result?
options: Unless heritable variation for tolerance exists or arises by mutation, selection cannot favor it, and the population may crash.
The beetles develop toxin tolerance within a generation or two, because they need the plant to survive.
Natural selection produces a new tolerance allele in the beetles that try hardest to eat the toxic plant.
Beetles that eat the plant adjust their digestion over their lives and pass that adjustment on to their offspring.

items.q: In lakes with trout, small fish called sticklebacks with more armor plates survive better than those with fewer plates; in lakes without trout, they do not. What is the selective pressure in this example?
options: Trout catching and eating sticklebacks
The alleles that control the number of plates
The armor plates on the sticklebacks' sides
The number of offspring each stickleback produces

items.q: Which statement about natural selection is correct?
options: It acts on individuals, but its effect is a change in the population's traits over generations.
It changes the inherited traits of individuals so that each one fits its environment better.
It acts on whole populations by making the individuals more similar within a single generation.
It works toward a goal: the best possible version of each trait for the environment a population lives in.

items.q: Which statement best describes the difference between birds hatched in 1976 and in 1978?
options: Mean beak depth rose by about 0.5 mm, and the error bars do not overlap, so the difference is likely real.
Mean beak depth rose by about 0.5 mm, but the error bars overlap, so the data do not show a real difference.
Mean beak depth rose by about 5 mm, which is larger than the year-to-year change at any later time.
Mean beak depth stayed about the same, because the change is smaller than the size of the error bars.

items.q: Calculate the percent change in mean beak depth from birds hatched in 1976 to birds hatched in 1978. Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which explanation best accounts for the deeper beaks of birds hatched in 1978?
options: In the drought, deep-beaked birds cracked the hard seeds left, survived and bred more, and their chicks inherited deep beaks.
Chicks hatched after the drought grew deeper beaks because their parents passed on the beak growth they gained by cracking hard seeds.
The drought caused mutations that made beaks deeper in the birds that needed to crack large, hard seeds to survive.
Birds hatched in 1978 ate harder seeds as chicks than birds hatched in 1976, and the extra work made their beaks grow deeper.

items.q: Mean beak depth fell for birds hatched in 1984 and 1985. What does this, together with the 1977 change, show about natural selection?
options: The favorable beak depth depends on the food supply, so selection reversed when the seeds changed.
Selection in the drought was too weak to last, so beak depth returned to its starting value after a few years.
Wet years cause mutations for smaller beaks, which undo the mutations for deeper beaks caused by the drought.
The population has one fixed best beak depth, and the 1984-1985 values show it drifting back toward that value.

items.q: Why was it important for the conclusion that the researchers had shown beak depth to be heritable?
options: Without it, survivors' deep beaks would not pass to their chicks, so selection could not explain the 1978 rise.
Heritability shows that the drought itself made the birds' beaks deeper, which is the main claim of the study.
Heritability means each chick has exactly its parents' beak depth, so no further measurements were needed.
Heritable traits are unaffected by the environment, which rules out any effect of the wet years after 1983.

items.q: What is the purpose of the cut-and-reglued group?
options: To test whether the handling itself affects mating success, with tail length unchanged
To provide birds with the longest possible tails for comparison with the lengthened group
To measure how much a male's tail feathers grow back in the four weeks after being cut
To give females a choice between males with natural tails and males with glued tails

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the error bars?
options: Lengthened males attracted more nests than the cut-and-reglued males, but the shortened males did not clearly differ from them.
Shortened males attracted fewer nests than the cut-and-reglued males, but the lengthened males did not clearly differ from them.
Each of the four groups differed clearly from each of the others in the number of nests.
No group clearly differed from any other, because each bar carries an error bar.

items.q: A tail half a meter long makes flying harder and may make males easier for predators to catch. Which explanation best accounts for long tails in this species?
options: Females prefer long-tailed males, and the extra matings outweigh the survival cost, so long-tail alleles spread.
Long tails help males escape predators by distracting them, so long-tailed males live longer than other males.
Females have long tails too, so the trait is favored in both sexes for the same reason.
Males grow longer tails during the breeding season because they need them to attract a female.

items.q: Assume tail length in males is heritable and females keep their preference. Predict the effect on each of these.

variables.name: Mean tail length of males, over many generations
Difference in tail length between males and females, over many generations
Natural tail length of the sons of a male whose tail was glued longer, compared with the sons of an unaltered male with the same natural tail

items.q: In an African finch, birds with small beaks feed efficiently on soft seeds and birds with large beaks crack hard seeds, but birds with mid-sized beaks handle both kinds poorly. If beak size is heritable, which pattern of selection is acting?
options: Disruptive selection, which favors both extremes and increases variation
Stabilizing selection, which favors the average and narrows variation
Directional selection, which favors the larger beaks and shifts the mean
Sexual selection, which favors the beak sizes preferred by mates

items.q: A study of more than 13,000 births in a London hospital between 1935 and 1946 found that babies of middle birth weight had the highest survival, and that survival fell for both lighter and heavier babies. If birth weight is partly heritable, which change in the distribution of birth weights would this selection tend to produce?
options: Little change in the mean, with fewer babies at both extremes
A shift of the mean toward heavier babies, as heavy babies survive
Two separate peaks, one of light and one of heavy babies
A wider spread, with more babies at both extremes

items.q: Which of these are abiotic selective pressures? Select ALL that apply.
options: Water temperature that is too cold for some fish to keep their enzymes working
Salty soil near a road treated in winter, which damages roots of some plants
A fungus that infects some frogs more easily than others
Hawks that catch mice more often when the mice stand out from the ground
Other plants in a meadow that shade the shorter seedlings

items.q: In an industrial region where most peppered moths were black, laws cut coal smoke, and lichen slowly grew back on the trees. Predict the change in each of these over the following decades.

variables.name: Percentage of moths in the region that are black
How easily birds spot a black moth resting on a tree trunk
Number of copies of the black allele in the cells of one black moth
Survival of pale moths compared with black moths

items.q: In a sooty woodland, researchers released 400 black and 400 pale marked moths and recaptured 82 black and 42 pale moths a week later. Calculate the survival of pale moths relative to black moths (proportion of pale recaptured ÷ proportion of black recaptured). Give your answer to two decimal places.

Deer mice living at 4,000 m carry hemoglobin variants, differing by a few amino acids, that bind oxygen more tightly than the hemoglobin of lowland deer mice. The variants are common at high altitude and rare in lowland populations. Which explanation best fits this pattern?
options: In thin air, tighter-binding hemoglobin loads more oxygen, so mice with it stay active and leave more offspring there.
Low oxygen at altitude caused mutations in the hemoglobin genes of each mouse living there, and the mice passed the changed genes on.
The mice's hemoglobin changed shape gradually during their lives at altitude, and the changed shape was inherited by their pups.
Tighter-binding hemoglobin helps mice at any altitude, so lowland populations will soon carry the variants too.

items.q: A scale-eating fish in an African lake has a mouth twisted either to the right or to the left; right-twisted fish attack prey from one side, left-twisted fish from the other, and the trait is inherited. Prey fish become watchful on the side from which they are attacked most often. In a year when 70% of the scale-eaters are right-twisted, what is the most likely result?
options: Left-twisted fish catch more scales and leave more offspring, so their share rises toward half.
Right-twisted fish keep the advantage of being common, so their share rises toward 100% over generations.
The two forms keep their current shares, because prey watch both sides equally.
Right-twisted fish switch the direction of their mouths so that they can attack from the less-watched side.

items.q: A student hypothesizes that the green color of a caterpillar is camouflage favored by birds that hunt by sight. Which experiment would best test this?
options: Put green and brown clay models on green leaves and on brown twigs, and count bird beak marks on each after two days.
Count how many green caterpillars live on one tree, and compare it with the number of birds that visit that tree each day.
Raise green caterpillars on green leaves and on brown leaves in the lab, and record whether their color changes as they grow.
Measure the amount of green pigment in caterpillars collected from several trees, and compare it with the number of leaves on each tree.

items.q: Alleles that keep the lactase gene active in adults are common in human populations with a long history of herding dairy animals and uncommon in populations without one. Which explanation best fits this pattern?
options: Where milk was a major food, adults who digested it got more energy and left more children.
Drinking milk as adults switched the lactase gene back on in herders, and the switched-on gene passed to their children.
Herding dairy animals caused mutations in the lactase gene that made adults able to digest milk sugar.
The alleles are favorable in any human population, but they happened to spread first among herders by chance.

items.q: Male elephant seals weigh up to about four times as much as females, and the largest males win fights for groups of females on breeding beaches. Which statement best explains the difference in size between the sexes?
options: Male competition for mates favors large males, who father most pups, so male size rises without the same pressure on females.
Females choose smaller partners to avoid being injured, so females stay small while males are selected to grow large.
Large size helps both sexes survive cold water equally, and males simply grow for more years than females do.
Males eat more than females during the breeding season, and the extra growth is passed on to their sons.

items.q: Which statement about adaptive traits is best supported by the history of peppered moths?
options: A trait that raises fitness in one environment can lower it in another.
Once a trait is favored, it remains favored in later generations.
A trait is adaptive when it helps an individual survive, even if it lowers reproduction.
A dark color is favorable for moths, wherever they live.

items.q: Which statement best describes the results?
options: The high line rose steadily, by about 15 percentage points; the low line fell fast, then leveled off.
Both lines changed at a steady rate, so the low line will reach 0% oil within a few more generations.
Both lines changed quickly at first and then stopped changing after about 30 generations.
The high line leveled off after 50 generations, while the low line kept falling at an even rate to the end.

items.q: Calculate the average rate of change in mean oil content in the high-oil line from generation 0 to generation 100, in percentage points per generation. Give your answer to two decimal places.
Which explanation best accounts for the high line still responding after 100 generations?
options: Oil content depends on many genes, so heritable variation remained for each round of selection.
Each generation the plants made more oil because they were grown in fields that suited high-oil corn.
The plants in the high line learned to store more oil, and passed what they learned to their kernels.
Choosing the 12 best ears each generation caused fresh mutations for high oil content in their kernels.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the leveling off of the low-oil line?
options: Kernels need some oil to grow, and most low-line plants already carried low-oil alleles, leaving little variation.
The breeders lost interest in the low line and stopped choosing the ears with the least oil after generation 30.
Corn has no alleles for less oil than the starting variety held, so the low line could not drop below 4.7%.
The low line was too small a population for selection to work, while the high line was a large one.

items.q: At generation 50, the researchers start a new line from the high-oil line and select it for LOW oil instead. Which result would show that the high-oil line still held heritable variation in oil content?
options: The new line's oil content falls, while the high line keeps rising.
The new line's oil content stays at 13.4%, the value of the high line at generation 50.
The new line's oil content drops to 4.7% within one generation and then stays there.
The new line's oil content keeps rising at the same rate as the high line.

items.q: By what factor did the MIC of treated flask 2 increase from day 0 to day 24? Give a whole number.
What do the untreated flasks allow the researchers to conclude?
options: The MIC rose because of the antibiotic, not because of 24 days of growth and transfer.
The antibiotic was strong enough to kill each cell in the treated flasks by day 24.
Bacteria grown without antibiotic mutate more slowly than bacteria exposed to it.
The cultures in the six flasks started with different levels of resistance to the drug.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the step-by-step rise in MIC in the treated flasks?
options: Cells whose random mutations raised resistance survived each higher dose and multiplied, again and again.
The antibiotic damaged DNA in a way that changed the drug's target, so the cells that it reached became resistant to it.
Each cell gradually got used to the antibiotic, and its tolerance was passed on when it divided.
The rising dose broke the antibiotic down faster, so later doses had less effect on the cells.

items.q: The three treated flasks were handled identically, yet on day 24 their MICs were 256, 512 and 128 µg/mL. Which explanation best fits this?
options: Resistance mutations arise at random, so each flask gained different mutations at different times.
The flasks probably received different doses, since identical handling should give identical results.
Flask 2 started with more resistant cells, because it was taken from the top of the starting culture.
Bacteria in flask 3 were less able to sense the antibiotic, so fewer of them changed.

items.q: What is the main difference between artificial selection and natural selection?
options: In artificial selection people decide which individuals breed; in natural selection the environment does.
Artificial selection acts on heritable variation; natural selection acts on traits gained during life.
Artificial selection creates alleles; natural selection acts on alleles that already exist.
Artificial selection changes individuals directly; natural selection changes populations over generations.

items.q: Kale, cabbage, broccoli and kohlrabi look very different, but they belong to one species and can be crossed. Which explanation best fits?
options: Farmers bred each crop from one wild mustard by selecting a different enlarged part.
Each crop arose from a different wild plant, and the crops later became one species by crossing.
The crops grow in different soils, which make the same plant grow into different shapes.
Each crop's shape came from one large mutation, which appeared when farmers first planted it.

items.q: Which are examples of unintended selection caused by people? Select ALL that apply.
options: Cod in a heavily fished sea begin to mature at smaller sizes over several decades.
More elephants are born without tusks after years of poaching for ivory.
A farmer saves seed from the tomato plants with the largest fruit to sow next spring.
A breeder mates the calmest horses in a herd to produce a gentler line.
A fish farm breeds the fastest-growing trout each year to raise more fish for sale.

items.q: A patient says, "The antibiotic made the bacteria in my infection mutate so they could resist it." Which response is most accurate?
options: Resistant cells were likely present by chance before treatment; the drug killed the rest, so they multiplied.
That is right: bacteria change their DNA in response to a drug, which is why resistance appears so quickly.
That is right for bacteria but not for animals, because bacteria can change their genes when they need to.
Resistance comes from the patient's immune system getting used to the antibiotic, not from the bacteria.

items.q: Why can antibiotic resistance spread through bacteria within a few years, while a change in a trait of a large mammal usually takes centuries or longer?
options: Bacteria reach huge numbers, divide quickly and share resistance genes, so variants arise and spread fast.
Bacteria are simpler, so one mutation can change any of their traits, while mammals lack the genes involved.
Mammals have no heritable variation, while bacteria have a great deal of it.
Bacteria evolve on purpose to survive drugs, while mammals change by chance over long periods.

items.q: In a fox-breeding experiment, only the calmest foxes were allowed to breed. Over many generations the foxes became tamer, and floppy ears and patchy coats, which nobody selected, also became common. Which explanation best fits?
options: Genes that affect tameness also affect ear and coat development, so those traits changed too.
The breeders secretly preferred foxes with floppy ears, so those foxes were chosen more often.
Living near people made the foxes' ears and coats change during their lives, and the changes were inherited.
Random mutations for floppy ears appeared because the foxes no longer needed upright ears.

items.q: Early farmers harvested teosinte, a wild grass whose ripe seeds fall from the plant. Seeds that fell before harvest were lost, so the farmers planted mainly seeds from plants that held on to them. They also planted seed from ears with the most kernels. Predict the change in each of these over many generations.

variables.name: Proportion of plants whose seeds stay on the ear until harvest
Mean number of kernels per ear
Number of chromosomes in each plant cell
Ability of the plants to spread their own seeds without people

items.q: An infection contains 4 × 10⁸ bacteria, of which 1 cell in 10⁶ is resistant to a drug. One day of treatment kills 99.9% of susceptible cells and no resistant cells. What percentage of the surviving cells is resistant? Give your answer to one decimal place.

In a population of bighorn sheep, hunters were allowed to shoot rams with the largest horns, and many of those rams were shot before they had bred much. Over 30 years, average horn size fell. Which explanation best fits?
options: Rams with smaller horns survived to father more lambs, so alleles for smaller horns became more common.
Hunting stressed the sheep, and the stress made each ram's horns grow less during its life.
Rams grew smaller horns because large horns had become dangerous to carry once hunting began.
The hunters' choice of target had no effect on the population, because horn size is set by the environment.

items.q: Many purebred dog breeds have high rates of particular inherited diseases. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Breeds began with few dogs and relatives are often mated, so recessive disease alleles end up homozygous.
Breeders selected for the diseases because they are linked to the looks that define each breed.
Purebred dogs mutate faster than mixed-breed dogs do, so over time they collect more disease alleles.
Diseases spread between dogs of the same breed because they live in kennels together.

items.q: Darwin used the work of animal and plant breeders as evidence for his theory. What does artificial selection show that supports the idea of natural selection?
options: Selection on heritable variation, over many generations, can greatly change a population.
Organisms change their traits when people need them to, and pass on the changes.
New species form whenever people breed animals for a few generations.
Selection can change any trait in a population, whether or not offspring inherit it.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data?
options: The small populations swung widely, and two reached 0 or 1; the large ones stayed near 0.5.
Frequencies in each population rose toward 1 over time, but the small populations got there sooner.
The small populations stayed near 0.5, while the large populations swung widely between 0.4 and 0.6.
Frequencies in the small populations fell toward 0, while those in the large populations rose toward 1.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the difference between the small and the large populations?
options: Ten parents carry 20 copies of the gene, a small sample that strays from the last generation by chance far more than 1,000 copies do.
The allele helps flies survive in small populations but harms them in large ones, so natural selection pushes the frequencies apart.
Flies in small populations mutate more often, so the eye-color allele is created and destroyed more often in them.
The large populations exchanged flies with one another, which kept their allele frequencies close to 0.5.

items.q: A student claims that allele e was favored by natural selection in population S1. Which evidence from the experiment best refutes this claim?
options: Population S2, of the same size and in the same conditions, lost allele e.
Allele e reached a frequency of 1 in population S1 by generation 15 of the experiment.
Population S1's frequency of allele e fell from 0.5 to 0.3 in the very first generation.
The large populations both ended the experiment with frequencies close to 0.5.

items.q: In generation 10, the frequency of allele e among the 10 parents of population S3 was 0.40. How many copies of allele e did those 10 parents carry? Give a whole number.
Suppose the experiment ran for 100 generations under the same conditions. Predict each of these, compared with generation 20.

variables.name: Share of heterozygous (Ee) flies in population S1
Share of heterozygous flies in population S3
Spread of allele frequencies among the five populations

items.q: Calculate the percent decrease in alleles per gene from 1960 to 1990. Give a positive number to one decimal place.
Which explanation best accounts for the fall in hatching success between 1960 and 1990?
options: In a small isolated group, drift and matings among relatives made harmful recessive alleles homozygous more often.
Birds in the small population chose to lay fewer eggs in each nest, so a smaller share of the eggs hatched.
The loss of prairie caused mutations in the birds that made their eggs less likely to hatch.
Fewer males displayed each spring, so many females could not find mates and laid unfertilized eggs instead.

items.q: Which process best explains the changes between 1990 and 1999?
options: Gene flow from the released birds restored lost alleles, so fewer embryos were homozygous for harmful ones.
The released birds outcompeted the local birds, so the local birds' alleles disappeared and were replaced.
Natural selection in the local population produced new alleles that let a larger share of the eggs hatch.
The larger number of birds raised the mutation rate, so genetic variation came back within a few years of release.

items.q: Prairie managers also burned and restored grassland in the same years the birds were released. Which addition to the study would best show that the released birds caused the recovery in hatching?
options: Monitoring a similar isolated population that got the grassland work but no birds
Counting the displaying males twice as often each spring in the same population
Measuring hatching in the three large source populations during those same years
Releasing another 270 birds later and checking whether hatching rises above 92%

items.q: A population of 200 snails contains 120 BB, 60 Bb and 20 bb individuals. Calculate the frequency of allele b. Give your answer to two decimal places.
In a sample of 50 deer mice, 20 are DD, 10 are Dd and 20 are dd. A student calculates the frequency of allele d as 20 ÷ 50 = 0.40. What is the correct frequency, and what did the student miss?
options: 0.50; the d alleles carried by the 10 heterozygotes, and the fact that each mouse has two copies
0.40; the student's method is correct for any population with a recessive allele
0.60; the student forgot to add the heterozygotes to the dd mice without halving them
0.20; the student should have divided by the total number of alleles, 100, without other changes

items.q: Which of these is an example of microevolution?
options: An allele for dark scales rises in frequency from 0.2 to 0.5 over 30 generations of lizards.
A lizard keeps growing larger each year of its life until it reaches its adult size.
A lizard darkens its skin on cold mornings and lightens it again on warm afternoons.
A lizard regrows a new tail after it loses its old one to a hungry predator.

items.q: Which process, by itself, changes the proportion of homozygous individuals in a population without changing its allele frequencies?
options: Nonrandom mating, such as self-fertilization
Gene flow from a population with different alleles
Genetic drift in a small population
Natural selection against one allele

items.q: A small, isolated population of mountain frogs has lost much of its genetic variation. Which events would increase genetic variation within this population? Select ALL that apply.
options: Frogs from a large lowland population move in and breed.
New mutations arise in the population over many generations.
A cold winter kills most of the frogs at random.
Frogs keep mating with close relatives for many generations.
The population stays at its present small size for 50 more generations.

items.q: A recessive form of dwarfism with extra fingers is far more common among the Old Order Amish of Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, than in most populations. This community descends from a few hundred settlers who arrived in the 1700s and mostly married within the community. Which explanation best fits?
options: Founder effect: a founder happened to carry the rare allele, and it became common in the small population.
Natural selection: the allele helped carriers survive the conditions of farm life in Pennsylvania.
Gene flow: the allele was brought in repeatedly by people who joined the community from outside.
Mutation: the community's farming way of life raised the rate of this particular mutation in its families.

items.q: Northern elephant seals were hunted to perhaps a few dozen animals in the 1890s. Protected since, they now number over 200,000, yet they have very little genetic variation. Why has the population's recovery not restored its variation?
options: The survivors held only some of the alleles; growth copies those, and new ones arise slowly by mutation.
Large populations lose variation faster than small ones do, so the population's growth itself removed alleles.
Hunting caused mutations that removed alleles from the seals that survived it.
The seals have had too little time since protection to relearn the traits their ancestors had before hunting.

items.q: A grass population grows on soil polluted with copper at an old mine, where copper-tolerant plants survive far better. Wind blows large amounts of pollen onto the mine from a big population of the same grass on clean soil nearby, where tolerance gives no advantage. What is the most likely effect of this pollen on the mine population?
options: It brings in copper-sensitivity alleles, so tolerance stays rarer on the mine than selection alone would make it.
It makes the mine plants more copper-tolerant, because the pollen comes from a larger population of grass.
It has no effect, because natural selection on the mine removes any sensitive seedlings at once.
It causes the clean-soil plants to become copper-tolerant, because pollen carries tolerance away from the mine.

items.q: Cheetahs carry so little genetic variation that skin grafted from one unrelated cheetah to another is often not rejected. Why does this worry conservation biologists, even though some cheetah populations are stable?
options: Fewer cheetahs are likely to carry alleles for surviving a new disease, so selection has less to work with.
Low variation means cheetahs reproduce poorly, so their populations are certain to decline within decades.
Animals with little genetic variation mutate faster, so harmful mutations will build up quickly in cheetahs.
Low variation makes cheetahs' skin grafts fail more often, which threatens their survival.

items.q: Which statement correctly contrasts genetic drift with natural selection?
options: Drift changes allele frequencies at random; selection changes them according to fitness.
Drift happens in large populations, while natural selection happens mainly in small populations.
Drift creates new alleles, while selection removes alleles that already exist.
Drift changes the traits of individuals, while selection changes the traits of whole populations.

items.q: Put the events of a founder effect in order.
options: A large mainland population carries a rare allele at a low frequency.
A storm carries a few individuals, one of them a carrier, to an empty island.
The founders' alleles, a small chance sample, form the island's whole gene pool.
The island population grows, with drift strong while it is small.
The allele that was rare on the mainland is common on the island.

items.q: Calculate p, the frequency of allele A, in population Y. Give your answer to two decimal places.
If population Y were in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with the allele frequencies it has, how many of its 500 plants would be expected to be Aa? Give a whole number.
Which population's genotype counts are closest to Hardy-Weinberg expectations?
options: Population X
Population Y
Population Z
The three are equally close, since each has 500 plants

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the genotype counts in population Y?
options: Selfing pairs like alleles, so homozygotes rise and heterozygotes fall while p and q stay the same.
Natural selection against heterozygotes removes Aa plants, which lowers the frequency of allele a in each generation.
Gene flow from bee-pollinated populations brings in extra AA and aa plants, so the cliff plants become homozygous.
The small cliff population has nearly lost allele a by genetic drift, so few of its plants can be heterozygous.

items.q: In population Z, p = 0.60 and q = 0.40. Which statement best explains its genotype counts?
options: Aa seedlings survive better than either homozygote, leaving more adult heterozygotes than 2pq predicts.
Plants in Z mate with relatives, which produces more heterozygotes than random mating would.
Allele A is dominant, so it pairs with allele a more often than chance and creates extra heterozygotes.
Population Z is in equilibrium, because its two allele frequencies add up to exactly 1 as they should.

items.q: Which population's results are consistent with Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for this gene?
options: Population 1
Population 2
Population 3
Population 4

items.q: In population 2, q fell by 0.25 in the first two generations but by less than 0.05 in the last ten. Which explanation best accounts for the slowdown?
options: As q falls, nearly all a alleles sit in Aa beetles, which look normal and are not removed.
The beetles adapted to the removal of aa beetles by producing fewer aa offspring each generation.
The researchers removed fewer reddish beetles in later generations because there were more beetles overall.
Mutation from A to a speeds up when q is low, adding back the a alleles removed by selection.

items.q: In population 2 at generation 8, q = 0.10, and the newly formed offspring are in Hardy-Weinberg proportions. What percentage of the a alleles in these offspring are carried by heterozygotes? Give a whole number.
If population 3 were kept the same way for another 100 generations, q would end up closest to which value?
Which Hardy-Weinberg condition is not met in population 4, and which feature of its graph supports this?
options: A very large population; q rises and falls at random instead of trending.
No natural selection; q falls steadily because reddish beetles die more often.
No gene flow; q moves toward the frequency in another stock of beetles.
Random mating; q stays at 0.50 while the share of heterozygous beetles falls.

items.q: In a population assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 9% of individuals show a recessive trait. What percentage of the population is expected to be homozygous dominant? Give a whole number.
A population of 800 frogs is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for a gene with p = 0.7. How many frogs are expected to be heterozygous? Give a whole number.

A student predicts that because allele B for brown fur is dominant, its frequency in a large, randomly mating mouse population with no selection will rise each generation until most mice are brown. Which response is correct?
options: Dominance sets which phenotype heterozygotes show; with no force acting, B's frequency stays constant.
The student is right, because heterozygotes look brown and so pass on the B allele more often than b.
The student is right, provided the starting frequency of B in the population is greater than 0.5.
The frequency of B will fall, because recessive alleles are hidden from selection in heterozygotes.

items.q: Which of these are conditions for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium? Select ALL that apply.
options: Mating is random with respect to genotype.
The population is very large.
No alleles enter or leave the population by gene flow.
Each genotype is present in equal numbers.
The dominant allele has a frequency above 0.5.
The alleles of the gene are codominant.

items.q: Researchers compare observed genotype counts in a lizard population with Hardy-Weinberg expectations and get χ² = 12.4, well above the critical value at p = 0.05. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The population departs from equilibrium, so a condition fails; these data alone do not show which.
The population is evolving by natural selection, because a large χ² shows that one genotype is fitter.
The population is in equilibrium, because a large χ² means the observed counts fit the expected counts well.
The allele frequencies were probably calculated wrongly, because real populations do not differ this much.

items.q: A large plant population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with q = 0.2. A change in its pollinators makes the plants start fertilizing themselves, with no selection, drift, gene flow or mutation. Predict the change in each of these over the next few generations.

variables.name: Frequency of allele a (q)
Proportion of heterozygous (Aa) plants
Proportion of aa plants

items.q: No real population meets all five Hardy-Weinberg conditions. Why are the equations still useful to biologists?
options: They predict what no evolution looks like, so a departure shows a process is acting and hints at which.
They predict the exact allele frequencies a population will have after several generations of selection.
They show that real populations do not evolve, because genotype frequencies in any population add up to 1.
They give the frequencies populations move toward over time, whatever processes act on them.

items.q: In a malaria region, newborns have sickle-cell genotypes that fit Hardy-Weinberg expectations, but a sample of adults from the same population has more heterozygotes than 2pq predicts. Which conclusion best fits these two observations?
options: Mating is random, but selection between birth and adulthood favors heterozygotes.
Mating is nonrandom, because adults choose partners with a different genotype from their own.
Drift has changed the allele frequencies between birth and adulthood, adding heterozygotes.
Gene flow brings heterozygous adults into the population, but no heterozygous newborns.

items.q: Which observation provides the best evidence that a population is NOT evolving at a particular gene?
options: Over five generations, q stays near 0.30 and genotype counts fit p², 2pq and q².
In one year's sample, genotype counts fit p², 2pq and q² with a small χ² value.
The dominant phenotype is more common than the recessive one in each of the years sampled.
The frequencies of the three genotypes add up to 1 in each year sampled.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the expected number of heterozygotes from genotype counts in order.
options: Count the copies of allele A: 2 × (number of AA) + (number of Aa).
Divide by 2 × the total number of individuals to get p.
Find q from q = 1 − p.
Calculate the expected frequency of heterozygotes, 2pq.
Multiply 2pq by the number of individuals.

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Humans share a more recent common ancestor with rhesus monkeys than with dogs.
Humans share a more recent common ancestor with chickens than with horses.
Tuna are more closely related to yeast than to humans.
Rabbits and dogs share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either does with humans.

items.q: What percentage of the 104 amino acid positions are identical in human and tuna cytochrome c? Give your answer to one decimal place.
A student concludes from the table that rabbits are more closely related to humans than dogs are. Which is the best evaluation of this claim?
options: It is weak: 9 and 11 differences are close, and one protein is a small sample, so more genes are needed.
It is strong: any difference in the number of amino acid changes reliably shows which species is more related.
It is strong, because rabbits and humans are both mammals, while dogs belong to a different group.
It is weak, because cytochrome c works in mitochondria, and mitochondrial proteins are not useful for comparing species.

items.q: Why do these data count as evidence of common ancestry?
options: Many sequences could do this job, yet species share one, with differences graded by relatedness.
Each species needs cytochrome c, so its sequence has to be identical across species for respiration to work.
The differences show that each species made its own version of the protein in response to its environment.
Species with more amino acid differences are better adapted than species with fewer differences.

items.q: A kangaroo is a mammal, more distantly related to humans than rabbits, dogs and horses are, but more closely related than birds. About how many differences from human cytochrome c would you predict for a kangaroo?
options: About 10
About 1
About 20
About 45

items.q: Put the horse-like fossils in order from oldest to youngest.
options: The dog-sized mammal with four front toes (layer 5)
The three-toed mammal (layer 3)
The one-toed mammal (layer 1)

items.q: What is the best estimate of the age of the three-toed fossils in layer 3?
options: Between 5.3 and 23 million years old
Exactly 14 million years, halfway between the ash layers
Older than 23 million years
Younger than 5.3 million years

items.q: The isotope used to date the ash has a half-life of 14 million years. What percentage of the original isotope should remain in the crystals of layer 6? Give your answer to two decimal places.
Why did the geologists date the ash layers rather than the fossil-bearing sandstone, shale and mudstone?
options: Ash crystals form as molten rock cools, starting the clock; sedimentary grains are older than the layer itself.
Sedimentary rocks contain no radioactive isotopes, so no radiometric method works on them.
Volcanic ash decays faster than sedimentary rock, so it gives a more precise age in fewer years.
Fossils are destroyed when sedimentary rock is heated, so the rock around them is not tested.

items.q: Which claim about the three fossils is best supported by these layers?
options: Horse-like mammals changed over time toward larger bodies and fewer toes: descent with modification.
Each fossil is the direct parent species of the fossil in the layer above it.
The one-toed mammal lived at the same time as the dog-sized mammal, but its fossils were buried higher.
The animals lost toes during their lives as they ran on harder ground, and passed the change on.

items.q: Which pair of structures is analogous rather than homologous?
options: The wing of a butterfly and the wing of a sparrow
The flipper of a whale and the arm of a human
The wing of a bat and the front leg of a cat
The pharyngeal arches of a fish embryo and of a human embryo

items.q: Which pairs are homologous structures? Select ALL that apply.
options: The flipper of a sea lion and the wing of a bat
The tailbone of a human and the tail of a monkey
The spines of a cactus and the thorns of a rose
The streamlined body of a shark and that of a dolphin
The wings of a bird and the wings of a housefly

items.q: Whales have small hip bones embedded in muscle and not attached to the spine. Which explanation best accounts for them?
options: Whales descend from four-legged land mammals, and these are reduced remnants of their hips.
The hip bones grew in each whale because it swam using its tail, which put stress on the lower body.
The hip bones are early stages of new legs that whales are evolving so they can return to land.
Whale hip bones formed separately in whales by convergent evolution with the hips of land animals.

items.q: Sharks and dolphins both have streamlined bodies, a dorsal fin and flippers or fins. Which explanation fits all the evidence best?
options: Similar selection for fast swimming shaped two unrelated groups alike: convergent evolution.
Sharks and dolphins inherited their body shapes from a recent common ancestor that was a streamlined fish.
Dolphins are fish that evolved lungs, so their shape shows their close relationship to sharks.
The body shapes are homologous, because structures with the same function are inherited.

items.q: Darwin noted that the animals of the Galápagos Islands resemble those of South America, about 1,000 km away, more than those of islands off Africa that have a similar climate. Which explanation best fits this pattern?
options: Galápagos species descend from colonists from nearby South America, modified over time on the islands.
Species are created to suit the climate where they live, so similar islands get similar species.
Animals that reach islands change their traits during their lives to match the island's climate.
South American species were carried to the Galápagos from Africa by people in historical times.

items.q: Human embryos, like fish embryos, develop a series of pharyngeal arches in the neck region. In fish these become supports for gills. What do they become in humans, and what does this indicate?
options: Parts of the jaw, middle ear and throat; a structure inherited from a common ancestor and modified in development
Working gills that the embryo uses before birth; humans pass through a fish stage of evolution in the womb
Nothing; they disappear before birth, which shows they are analogous to the gill arches of fish
Lungs; the arches turn into lungs, showing that lungs evolved from gills in a single step

items.q: Lobe-finned fish fossils are found in rocks about 385 million years old, and the earliest four-limbed animals in rocks about 365 million years old. Researchers want to find an animal with features of both. Which search plan is best supported by the evidence?
options: Search sedimentary rocks about 375 million years old that formed in shallow streams or coasts.
Search volcanic rocks about 375 million years old, which preserve fossils best.
Search rocks younger than 365 million years, where four-limbed animals are most common.
Search rocks of any age, because fossils of transitional forms are spread evenly through time.

items.q: A piece of charcoal from an ancient campfire contains 12.5% of the carbon-14 found in living wood. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5,730 years. How old is the charcoal? Give a whole number of years.
Why are transitional fossils, showing features of both an older and a later group, relatively rare?
options: Fossils form only under special conditions, such as quick burial, and most remains decay first.
Transitional forms did not exist, because new groups appear fully formed.
Transitional forms were too weak to survive for long, so very few individuals lived.
Fossils of transitional forms are destroyed faster than other fossils, because they are mixtures.

items.q: In rock layers around the world, many types of marine and land fossils that are common below a certain thin layer are absent from every layer above it. What does this pattern best indicate?
options: A mass extinction: many groups died out worldwide in a geologically short time.
A period of rapid fossil formation, when many new groups first appeared at once.
An error in relative dating, because fossil groups do not disappear from the record.
A time when the animals moved to places where rocks do not form.
